title: 10 Things We Know About Testing
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton names a new favourite paper on retrieval, the 2021 meta-analysis by Yang and colleagues, which reviews 222 classroom-based studies across subjects and phases, and uses it to answer ten practical questions. The findings are that testing boosts attainment compared with restudying, that format does not need to match the final exam, and that corrective feedback roughly doubles the benefit. More tests help, retrieval should be long and consistent, and the effect holds across ages, genders and subjects. Testing is not limited to facts, since it supports comprehension and application, and low stakes work as well as high stakes while reducing anxiety. Barton adds his own reflections, such as including harder questions in retrieval and moving away from tidy unit-end assessments, and describes his own shift to unrecorded self-marked quizzes. The post ends with a description of the retrieval feature on Eedi, which is promotional but a small part of the whole.
points: Yang et al.'s review of 222 classroom studies shows a testing effect of about 0.5, with benefits regardless of test format, so variety is encouraged.
Corrective feedback after quizzing roughly doubles the benefit and stops misconceptions embedding.
Retrieval should be frequent and spread over long periods, not confined to a unit, with early recall in the next Do Now and later spaced opportunities.
Retrieval is not just for facts; it supports comprehension and application, and Barton argues for including challenging questions so depth is not limited to initial teaching.
Low-stakes quizzes yield the same learning as high-stakes ones with less anxiety; infrequent high-stakes unit tests offer too few retrieval chances.
quotes: Oh, and please don’t be put off by the word test in the title. Think instead of retrieval opportunities. In other words, the times we challenge students to think hard about concepts they have met in the past.
Sure, this feels much more challenging than simply re-reading notes or watching a video, but it is that very effort that cements the knowledge into long-term memory.
First, the format of the retrieval opportunity does not need to match the format of the end exam. Second, this gives us an opportunity to vary the format of our retrieval opportunities.
This stops misconceptions from becoming embedded, and also provides the students with an opportunity to pause, reflect and self-explain.

The key point here is that we need to move away from teaching and assessing concepts in a nice tidy box before moving on to the next idea. For retrieval to be effective, it needs to be for the long term.

Indeed, in Tips for Teachers, I argue that you should include more challenging questions in retrieval opportunities, otherwise the only chance students have to think deep about a concept is when the concept is first being taught.
One way to think about this is that without facts at their disposal, it is very difficult for students to engage in any higher-order thinking as they have nothing to build that thinking upon.
